title: Claude cannot make highly detailed levels
author: NeverLucky159
selftext:
I asked Claude to replicate this exact environment in Godot to make a game level where my character would run and fight, including all the little details, cracks in the floor, water reflections etc.

He simply told me that I will have to make it all by myself in a 3D software or if he makes it, it won't look even close to my reference. This was Fable 5.2 on high

So is this the limit of current AI? It can create only very simple levels with not so much detail?   
And would there be a way to use this as a level by using the image itself as 2D with some tricks of putting 3D lights somewhere.. not sure if that would work at all

comments.author: aj_marshall
comments.body:
Claude can certainly assist you in making this in Godot, but yes- Fable 5.2 is not a model capable of direct 3D model generation through diffusion. It can make 3D assets in Blender via an MCP (which I recommend trying) and even assemble those assets into a level once you have them. However, it won't be a "one shot" kind of deal. You'll need to spend time prompting for shaders, textures, so on and so forth. 

Part of using AI to assist you in game development is also learning the game development process.

You can't use AI to "one shot" a game.

replies.author: Kepler___
replies.body:
Spot on. I've heard it called a "Councel of experts" approach. Because how how LLMs are designed, specialized models are going to be superior at their specialization. 

Follwing is for OP: Claude is your engineer, great coding agent but i'd hesitate to let him paint my wall, let alone level. Create concept art in something like gpt, feed to modeler like trellis if your working locally, meshy if you have a few bucks, then ether hand fix/craft elements or ask Claude to touch up in blender. 

Entire levels will also look like slop if you try to fit the entire thing through this pipeline. Building smaller bits and then combining them (Claude can absolutly do this when you have the GLBs if you want, but its a nice spot to add hand crafting) is the way to go. The smaller the better. In my current project I've broken it down all the way to individual walls that I can use to build custom structures, adding in details like pots and rugs after. 

I'm gabbing too much at this point, but I feel like i have to add that lighting will be a learning process. Meshs will have tears that need to be addressed, Claude will try to hard code everything in the most bizzare way if given leeway (mother fucker is ALLERGIC to using nodes in Godot unless asked) so this will be the hardest part of the process, but probably not nearly as hard as you would expect going in.

A useful thing to keep in mind is that the majority of people commenting about video game development and AI:

replies.author: Disastrous-Gain5870
replies.body: It’s not just a single prompt, like I said it’s constant iterations. Your first prompt is just the base/prototype basically. I don’t use prefabs, I first get Claude to make the level with code, then over time I’ll both polish it and have Claude remake certain parts in Blender. It’s not something that can be done in a single day unless you want it to be low quality. I’m making a procedural 2D level creator right now and I’ve been working on it for close to a month. For a single level, it should take much less time however. I think a single level could be done in a few days. Still, it will require much more than a single prompt.

comments.author: Kindly-Sail6260
comments.body:
Claude can do that on Opus 5.5 with direction. You just have to know what goes into games with high levels of design. Green cracks on the floor can be as simple as decals or a dedicated mesh with that. Most of what you see are broken up into modular pieces that were carefully designed to fit into one another. Trim sheets, procedural materials, mesh blending, creating 3d objects with normals for a higher quality look without sacrificing performance. And we’re only scratching the surface as to how you go about it. You have to ask Fable to research how these games are made and guarantee you, you’ll get a closer version of what you want. It just takes dozens of dozens of assets to get the look you’re going. 

That’s why I always harp that if you don’t know anything about game development, start small and learn as you go. Instead of wanting this beautiful crazy look, why not gray box the level design or procedural flow? Why not design the combat so it’s so engaging that the environment doesn’t matter much? From this post, it looks like you’re working backwards rather than at the first step. 

Game feel is the most important aspect of the game. This is the largest complaint by players everywhere. It’s a beautifully packaged nothing burger. They’re tired of that. They want fun games first. Get that right and the level will literally flesh itself out on its own. Heed these words. 

Also work on your prompts big bro. You got this.
